mainEntity.name: How long do different types of dental implants typically last?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most dental implants, particularly endosteal titanium implants, can last 20 years or longer with proper care in many patients. The implant crown may need replacement after 10-15 years due to normal wear, but the implant itself often remains stable for decades. Success rates are generally high in clinical studies, though individual outcomes depend on a range of clinical and patient factors.

mainEntity.name: Are there any restrictions on who can have certain types of implants?

acceptedAnswer.text: Patient suitability varies by implant type and individual circumstances. Endosteal implants require adequate bone volume and density, whilst certain medical conditions may affect healing. Age isn't typically a barrier, but growing adolescents may need to wait until jaw development is complete. Your dental team will assess factors including bone health, medical history, and oral hygiene to determine the most appropriate approach.

mainEntity.name: What's the difference in recovery time between implant types?

acceptedAnswer.text: Endosteal implants typically require 3-6 months for osseointegration before final restoration. Subperiosteal implants may have shorter initial healing periods but can have different long-term adaptation phases. Multiple implants or complex cases may require longer healing times. Individual factors such as bone quality, overall health, and post-operative care significantly influence recovery duration.

mainEntity.name: Can implant types be combined in the same treatment?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, different implant approaches can be combined within the same treatment plan. For example, different sized endosteal implants might be used in various locations, or immediate and delayed loading protocols might be combined. Treatment planning considers each area's specific requirements to optimise overall success and function.

mainEntity.name: How do I know which implant type is right for my situation?

acceptedAnswer.text: Implant selection requires comprehensive clinical examination including X-rays or CT scans to assess bone volume and quality. Your dentist will consider factors such as the number and location of missing teeth, bone health, gum condition, bite forces, aesthetic requirements, and your overall health. This assessment determines the most appropriate implant type and treatment approach for your individual circumstances.

mainEntity.name: What happens if my bone isn't suitable for standard implants?

acceptedAnswer.text: Insufficient bone doesn't necessarily prevent implant treatment. Options include bone grafting procedures to augment existing bone, shorter or narrower implant designs, alternative placement techniques, or subperiosteal implants in specific cases. Advanced techniques such as sinus lifts or ridge augmentation can create suitable conditions for implant placement. Bone augmentation specialists can evaluate complex cases and recommend appropriate approaches.
